title: Living Stones and the Suffering Shepherd
summary: Reborn believers crave the Lord, are built into God’s priestly house, live honorably among unbelievers, and follow Christ’s steps through unjust suffering.
historicalContext: The churches of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia were made up largely of people who had turned from idols to the living God (1 Peter 4:3-4). Conversion had cost them social standing. Refusing the temple feasts, guild banquets, and household gods of their towns, they appeared disloyal and strange, and neighbors accused them of wrongdoing. Many lived without civic rights, and some were household slaves under unbelieving masters who could beat them without legal restraint. Rome governed through an emperor and provincial governors, and the empire prized order and conformity. Into this setting Peter writes that a people despised by their society are, in God’s sight, a temple, a priesthood, and a nation of his own. He then shows how such a people should live under rulers and masters whose authority they cannot control, keeping their eyes on Christ, who suffered unjustly before them.
literaryContext: Chapter 2 hinges on the new birth announced in 1:22-25. Its first verses draw the ethical consequence: those born of the abiding word must lay aside the vices that destroy love and crave the Lord as infants crave milk. Peter then gathers a chain of Old Testament texts about a stone (Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 8:14) and about God’s covenant people (Exodus 19:5-6; Isaiah 43:20-21; Hosea 2:23) to describe the church’s identity in Christ. Verses 11-12 open the main body of the letter, which runs to 4:11, and state its program: live as pilgrims whose good conduct answers slander. The household instructions that follow begin with civic duty and then address slaves, whose unjust suffering leads into the chapter’s climax, a meditation on Christ as Isaiah’s Suffering Servant. The chapter thus moves from identity to conduct and grounds both in the cross.
themes: Spiritual growth through craving the Lord
Christ the living, rejected, and exalted stone
The church as God’s temple and priesthood
Free submission for the Lord’s sake
Following Christ’s steps in unjust suffering

outline.title: Growing as Newborn Children
outline.summary: Those born again lay aside the vices that wound fellowship and long for the nourishment that comes from the gracious Lord.

outline.title: The Living Stone and God’s Own People
outline.summary: Coming to Christ, the stone rejected by men and chosen by God, believers become a spiritual house, a royal priesthood, and a people who proclaim his mercy.

outline.title: Pilgrims Among the Nations
outline.summary: As strangers in the world, believers resist the desires that wage war on them and live so well that slanderers may come to glorify God.

outline.title: Free Servants Under Human Authority
outline.summary: For the Lord’s sake believers honor the institutions of government, silencing ignorance by doing good while reserving their fear for God alone.

outline.title: Following the Suffering Servant
outline.summary: Household slaves who endure unjust treatment follow the pattern of Christ, who bore sins on the cross and gathers straying sheep to himself as Shepherd and Overseer.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore” ties the command to what Peter has just said. His readers have been born again of incorruptible seed, by the word that endures forever (1:23-25), and they have been told to love one another “with a pure heart fervently” (1:22). New birth and brotherly love lead directly to a list of things that must go. The verb pictures removing clothing, as a person strips off soiled garments before putting on clean ones. The same imagery appears when Paul urges believers to put off the old self and put on the new (Colossians 3:8-10).

The five vices form a sequence. “Malice” is settled ill will, the wish for harm to another. “Guile” is deceit, the bait that hides the hook. “Hypocrisies” describes playing a part, presenting a face that the heart does not match. “Envies” are resentments at another’s good, and “evil speakings” are the backbiting and disparaging talk that spread behind someone’s back. The movement runs from hidden motive to spoken word, from what festers inside to what wounds others in public.

Every item on the list attacks the love Peter has just commanded. A congregation already pressed by hostile neighbors cannot afford to be torn from within. Peter repeats “all” three times, allowing no reserve of tolerated spite. Guile appears here at the start of the chapter and returns near its end, where Christ is the one in whose mouth no guile was found (2:22). Laying aside these things is therefore more than self-improvement; it is the reshaping of a life after the likeness of the Lord who called them.

wordNotes.term: ἀποθέμενοι (apothemenoi) — laying aside
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes putting off something as one removes a garment. It depends on the command “desire” in verse 2 and carries the force of an instruction: having stripped away these vices, crave the Lord’s nourishment. The image implies a decisive break rather than gradual tinkering.

wordNotes.term: καταλαλιάς (katalalias) — evil speakings
wordNotes.explanation: The word refers to speaking against others, especially slander and disparaging talk carried on in their absence. Peter later uses the related verb for the way unbelievers speak against Christians (2:12; 3:16). Believers must not treat one another as the world treats them.

verses.bibleText: As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The main command of verses 1-3 is “desire.” Peter chooses a strong verb for longing, the kind of hunger that cannot be distracted. “As newborn babes” continues the image of new birth from 1:3 and 1:23. He does not imply that his readers are recent converts or spiritually immature. Every believer, however long in the faith, is to want God’s nourishment the way an infant wants milk: instinctively, constantly, and with the whole self.

The milk is described with two adjectives. The KJV’s “sincere” renders a word meaning “without guile,” and it forms a deliberate echo of verse 1. Having put away all guile, believers crave what has no guile in it, food that is pure and unadulterated. The phrase “of the word” translates an adjective that can mean “spiritual” or “reasonable,” but its sound links it to the “word of God” in 1:23-25. Peter has in view the nourishment God supplies through his living word, which brings believers into contact with the Lord himself (2:3).

Paul and the letter to the Hebrews use milk for elementary teaching that should give way to solid food (1 Corinthians 3:2; Hebrews 5:12-14). Peter’s image works differently. Here milk is simply what keeps a newborn alive and growing, and no stage of Christian life outgrows the need for it.

The goal is growth. Many manuscripts read “that ye may grow thereby unto salvation,” and that fuller wording fits the letter well. Salvation is a gift already received and also an inheritance “ready to be revealed in the last time” (1:5). Growth fed by God’s word prepares believers for that day. The process is grace from first to last: God gives the life, God supplies the food, and the believer’s part is to want it and receive it.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιποθήσατε (epipothēsate) — desire
wordNotes.explanation: The verb expresses intense longing. The psalmist uses its family of words for the soul that pants after God, and Paul for his yearning to see beloved believers. Peter commands such longing for spiritual nourishment, assuming that new life naturally hungers and that this hunger should be cultivated.

wordNotes.term: λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα (logikon adolon gala) — the sincere milk of the word
wordNotes.explanation: Adolos means free of deceit or adulteration and plays on dolos, “guile,” in verse 1. Logikos can mean “spiritual” or “rational,” while its connection with logos recalls the living word of 1:23-25. Together they describe pure nourishment that comes from God’s word and suits those born of it.

verses.bibleText: If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter draws his wording from Psalm 34:8: “O taste and see that the LORD is good.” He will return to the same psalm in 3:10-12, which suggests it was a favorite text for him and for believers who suffered. David wrote it after escaping danger, and it celebrates God’s care for the afflicted who take refuge in him.

“If so be” does not express doubt. The construction assumes the condition is true: since you have tasted that the Lord is gracious, keep longing for more. A taste is personal experience, not report or rumor. These believers came to know the Lord’s kindness when the gospel reached them, and that first experience becomes the reason to keep coming back. Appetite grows by being fed.

“Gracious” renders a word meaning kind, good, or beneficial. Jesus used it when he said God is kind to the unthankful and the evil (Luke 6:35). Its sound is also close to the title “Christ,” and early readers may have caught the echo.

In the psalm “the LORD” is the covenant name of Israel’s God. Peter immediately identifies this Lord as the one “to whom coming” believers find the living stone (2:4), that is, Jesus Christ. Without argument, he applies to Jesus a text about the LORD himself, a quiet witness to Christ’s full deity.

wordNotes.term: χρηστὸς ὁ κύριος (chrēstos ho kyrios) — the Lord is gracious
wordNotes.explanation: Chrēstos describes goodness that shows itself in kindness and generosity. Taken from Psalm 34:8 LXX, the phrase invites trust in a Lord who is good to those who come to him. Peter applies the psalm’s “Lord” to Jesus Christ.

verses.bibleText: To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“To whom coming” continues from the gracious Lord of verse 3. The participle is in the present tense, describing a continual approach rather than a single moment of conversion. In the Greek Old Testament the same verb is used for drawing near to God in worship, and Psalm 34, which Peter has just quoted, invites people to come to the Lord and be enlightened. Believers keep coming to Christ as a hungry child keeps returning for nourishment.

He is “a living stone.” Stone imagery for God and his Messiah runs through the Old Testament: the rock of Israel, the tested cornerstone of Isaiah 28:16, the rejected stone of Psalm 118:22, the stone cut without hands that fills the earth in Daniel 2. Peter adds the adjective “living.” A stone is normally the very picture of lifelessness, but this stone was raised from the dead and now gives life. The word ties back to the “lively hope” of 1:3 and the word that “liveth” in 1:23.

“Disallowed indeed of men” translates a verb that means to reject after examination, as builders test a stone and throw it aside as unfit. Jesus used this word when he foretold that he would be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes (Mark 8:31). People looked at him and decided he was not the kind of Messiah they wanted.

God’s verdict reversed theirs. He is “chosen of God, and precious,” elect and held in honor. That contrast speaks directly to Peter’s readers, who were themselves being examined and rejected by their neighbors. The judgment of society is not final. What matters is God’s estimate, and the One they follow was despised by men before he was vindicated by God.

The apostle whose own name meant “rock” claims no place in this building for himself. All attention goes to Christ as the foundation stone.

wordNotes.term: ἀποδεδοκιμασμένον (apodedokimasmenon) — disallowed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes rejection after testing, the decision that something fails to meet the required standard. It is the word of Psalm 118:22 LXX for the builders’ rejection of the stone, and Jesus used it of his coming rejection. The perfect participle suggests a settled verdict.

wordNotes.term: λίθον ζῶντα (lithon zōnta) — a living stone
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase joins an image of permanence with an affirmation of life. Christ is the stone of prophecy, and he is alive through resurrection. Those joined to him share that life, as verse 5 immediately states.

verses.bibleText: Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Ye also, as lively stones” applies to believers the very adjective just used of Christ. They are living stones because they are joined to the living Stone. Their life is derived, received by union with him, much as branches live from the vine (John 15:5).

They “are built up a spiritual house.” The verb can be read as a statement (“you are being built”) or as an invitation (“let yourselves be built”). Either way, God is the builder and believers are the material he shapes and sets in place. “House” is a common Old Testament term for the temple, the house of the Lord (2 Samuel 7:13; 1 Kings 8:10-13), and Peter will later call the church “the house of God” (4:17). The temple in Jerusalem was probably still standing when he wrote, yet he describes a temple of people, indwelt by the Spirit. The house is singular and the stones are plural. No believer is a temple by himself; each is fitted into a structure with others.

Within this house the believers are also “an holy priesthood.” Under the old covenant only the sons of Aaron could approach the altar. Now the whole community has access to God. That access does not bypass Christ. It exists because he is the one Mediator and the great High Priest who has passed into the heavens and ministers in the true sanctuary (Hebrews 4:14-16; 8:1-2). Through his priesthood every believer may come boldly to the throne of grace without another human mediator.

A priesthood offers sacrifices, and these are “spiritual sacrifices.” The animal sacrifices pointed to Christ and found their fulfillment in his death. What remains for his people to offer is the dedicated life: bodies presented as living sacrifices (Romans 12:1), the praise of lips that confess his name, doing good and sharing with others (Hebrews 13:15-16), a broken and contrite heart (Psalm 51:17). The word “spiritual” here means produced and governed by the Spirit, not unreal or merely inward.

Such offerings are “acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.” Even the best worship of believers is imperfect. It is received because it rises to God through the merit and mediation of his Son. The church’s worship, service, and witness are a priestly ministry carried out in his name, and all of it depends on him.

wordNotes.term: ἱεράτευμα ἅγιον (hierateuma hagion) — an holy priesthood
wordNotes.explanation: Hierateuma describes a body of priests functioning together. The term comes from Exodus 19:6, where God called Israel to be a kingdom of priests. Peter applies the calling to the whole church: every believer has access to God through Christ and serves as priest in worship and witness, while Christ alone remains the High Priest whose mediation makes that access possible.

wordNotes.term: πνευματικὰς θυσίας (pneumatikas thysias) — spiritual sacrifices
wordNotes.explanation: These are offerings shaped by the Holy Spirit rather than by the altar ritual. Scripture names them as praise, thanksgiving, generosity, obedience, and the surrender of the whole person to God. They are not offered to obtain forgiveness, which Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice secured, but in grateful worship.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now supports his teaching with Scripture: “it is contained in the scripture.” The first text is Isaiah 28:16. In Isaiah’s day the rulers of Jerusalem trusted political alliances and boasted that they had made a covenant with death that would protect them. God answered that he himself would lay in Zion a tried and precious cornerstone, and that the one who relied on it would stand when every false refuge was swept away. True security lay in what God had established, never in human schemes.

Peter reads the prophecy as fulfilled in Jesus. “Behold, I lay” stresses divine initiative: God, not human builders, chose and placed this stone. “Sion,” the hill of the temple and the city of God, is the place of his dwelling with his people. The new temple of verse 5 rises on this foundation.

“A chief corner stone” describes the stone set at the corner of a foundation, the one that fixes the lines for every wall and binds the structure together. Paul uses the same word when he describes the church as a holy temple built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ himself as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). Everything in the building takes its alignment from him. He is “elect, precious,” the same words of verse 4.

The promise is personal: “he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.” Faith rests on a person. To be “confounded” is to be put to shame, to have one’s confidence exposed as empty. Peter’s readers were being shamed by their neighbors, but those who trust Christ will never be disgraced before God. Paul quotes the same line twice (Romans 9:33; 10:11), extending it to everyone who calls on the name of the Lord.

wordNotes.term: ἀκρογωνιαῖον (akrogōniaion) — chief corner stone
wordNotes.explanation: The term designates the principal stone at the corner of a building, laid first so that the rest of the structure follows its lines. Applied to Christ, it means that the whole church takes its direction, stability, and unity from him.

wordNotes.term: οὐ μὴ καταισχυνθῇ (ou mē kataischynthē) — shall not be confounded
wordNotes.explanation: The double negative is emphatic: the believer will by no means be put to shame. The verb speaks of disgrace that comes when trust proves misplaced. In the context of final judgment, the promise assures believers that their confidence in Christ will be vindicated.

verses.bibleText: Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Unto you therefore which believe he is precious.” The Greek is compact and can be rendered, “To you who believe, then, is the honor.” Both senses belong together. Christ is precious to those who trust him, and because they trust him they share the honor God has given him. Isaiah promised that the believer would not be put to shame (2:6); Peter states the positive side of that promise. People who are mocked as members of a strange sect are, in God’s reckoning, honored by their union with his chosen Stone.

The verse then turns to “them which be disobedient.” Some manuscripts read “unbelieving,” and in Peter’s thought the two belong together. Refusing to believe the gospel is itself disobedience to God’s call, and disobedience grows from unbelief.

For such people Peter cites Psalm 118:22: “the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner.” The psalm celebrates a festal procession in which the Lord’s rejected one is vindicated, and it contains the cry “Hosanna” that greeted Jesus on his way into Jerusalem. After the parable of the vineyard, Jesus applied this verse to himself (Matthew 21:42). Peter used it before the Sanhedrin to declare that the crucified Jesus, whom they had set aside, was now raised by God (Acts 4:10-11).

The builders were first of all the leaders who should have recognized Israel’s Messiah. The principle reaches further. Anyone who builds a life without Christ has rejected the stone on which everything depends. Their rejection does not remove him from his place. God has already made him the head of the corner.

wordNotes.term: ἡ τιμή (hē timē) — he is precious
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the honor,” the noun corresponds to the adjective “precious” in verses 4 and 6. Believers receive the honor that belongs to the chosen Stone instead of the shame Isaiah says they will be spared. Christ is their treasure, and in him they are honored before God.

wordNotes.term: κεφαλὴν γωνίας (kephalēn gōnias) — head of the corner
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase from Psalm 118:22 names the stone that holds the decisive position in a building, whether the cornerstone of the foundation or the capstone above. In either case the stone once discarded now occupies the place of greatest importance, a picture of Christ’s resurrection and exaltation.

verses.bibleText: And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third stone text comes from Isaiah 8:14. In that passage the LORD himself would be a sanctuary for those who feared him and “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence” to both houses of Israel that refused his word. Once again Peter takes a passage about the LORD and applies it without hesitation to Jesus. The same Christ is a refuge to one person and an obstacle to another, depending on how each responds to him.

“A stone of stumbling” describes a stone that trips the traveler. “A rock of offence” uses a word that originally meant the trigger of a trap and came to mean anything that causes a person to fall. Simeon foresaw it when he said the child Jesus was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel (Luke 2:34). The stumbling is serious; it describes a fall that ends in ruin.

Peter explains why people stumble: they “stumble at the word, being disobedient.” The cause lies in their refusal of the message, not in any defect of the stone. The gospel that offers life becomes the occasion of their fall because they will not obey it.

“Whereunto also they were appointed” has often been read as though God decreed in advance that certain people must disbelieve. The verse does not say that. The verb “appointed” is the same one translated “I lay” in verse 6: God placed the stone in Zion. In placing Christ there, God also fixed the two outcomes that follow from response to him. Those who believe receive honor; those who persist in disobedience fall. What is appointed is the stumbling that comes to the disobedient, the sure consequence of rejecting Christ. This fits Peter’s description of election as “according to the foreknowledge of God” (1:2) and his later testimony that the Lord is “not willing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

For readers who faced the hostility of neighbors, this was steadying. Rejection of Christ by many did not mean the gospel had failed. Scripture had foretold it, and God remained in control of its outcome.

wordNotes.term: πρόσκομμα … σκάνδαλον (proskomma … skandalon) — stumbling … offence
wordNotes.explanation: Proskomma is an obstacle against which one strikes the foot. Skandalon was originally the bait stick of a trap and came to mean whatever causes someone to fall. Paired here from Isaiah 8:14, the words describe Christ as the decisive point at which unbelief comes to grief.

wordNotes.term: εἰς ὃ καὶ ἐτέθησαν (eis ho kai etethēsan) — whereunto also they were appointed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb tithēmi is the same used for God “laying” the stone in verse 6. What God has set is the outcome of disobedience: those who reject the word will stumble. The text names the appointed consequence of unbelief, not a decree that compels anyone to refuse the gospel.

verses.bibleText: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But ye” sets believers over against those who stumble. Peter now gathers titles that God once gave Israel and gives them to the church. Most of them come from Exodus 19:5-6, spoken at Sinai after the exodus, and from Isaiah 43:20-21, where God promises a new exodus for his people. The church stands in continuity with the covenant people. Gentile believers have been joined, with the believing remnant of Israel, to the one people of promise (Romans 11:17; Ephesians 2:12-13).

“A chosen generation” means a chosen race or kind. Membership comes by new birth (1:23), not by ancestry, and it unites people of every background. Their neighbors regarded them as an odd new kind of people; Peter says they are a kind chosen by God.

“A royal priesthood” comes from the Greek of Exodus 19:6. The phrase describes a priesthood that belongs to the King and shares his reign. Revelation celebrates the same calling when it says Christ has made his people kings and priests unto God (Revelation 1:6; 5:10). Verse 5 described this priesthood offering sacrifices to God; here it represents God before the nations.

“An holy nation” is a people set apart, governed by God’s law and reflecting his character. “A peculiar people” uses older English in which “peculiar” meant one’s own private property. The Greek speaks of a people for God’s own possession, a treasured people he has acquired (Malachi 3:17; Titus 2:14).

These privileges carry a purpose: “that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you.” The word translated “praises” refers to God’s excellencies, especially his mighty acts of salvation. Israel was redeemed from Egypt to declare what God had done. The church has been redeemed by Christ to proclaim his saving deeds to the world. Worship and witness belong together.

The call is “out of darkness into his marvellous light.” Darkness describes ignorance of God, bondage to sin, and the futile way of life inherited from the past (1:18). Light is the truth and presence of God. As God commanded light to shine at creation, he has shone into the hearts of believers to give the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Conversion is a new exodus and a new creation.

wordNotes.term: λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν (laos eis peripoiēsin) — a peculiar people
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase means a people acquired as God’s own possession. It echoes God’s description of Israel as his treasured possession. The KJV’s “peculiar” carried the older sense of personal property, not strangeness. The church belongs to God, purchased by the blood of his Son.

wordNotes.term: τὰς ἀρετὰς ἐξαγγείλητε (tas aretas exangeilēte) — shew forth the praises
wordNotes.explanation: Aretai refers to excellencies, particularly God’s glorious deeds of deliverance. The verb means to proclaim openly. Drawn from Isaiah 43:21, the phrase gives God’s people a mission of declaring his saving acts in word and in life.

verses.bibleText: Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter closes the section with an echo of Hosea. The prophet was told to name his children Lo-ruhamah, “not pitied,” and Lo-ammi, “not my people,” as signs of God’s judgment on the unfaithful northern kingdom (Hosea 1:6-9). Yet the same prophecy promised reversal: God would have mercy on the one not pitied and say to those not his people, “Thou art my people” (Hosea 2:23).

Peter applies that promise to his readers, most of whom had come from paganism (4:3-4). Paul does the same in Romans 9:25-26, seeing in Hosea’s words God’s purpose to call Gentiles. The prophet’s hope for wayward Israel opened outward to include nations that had never known God.

The verse turns on “in time past” and “now.” Before the gospel reached them, these believers belonged to no covenant people and had no claim on God’s mercy. Now they are “the people of God.” Their identity has been transferred. The last clause reads literally, “who had not been shown mercy, but now have been shown mercy.” Mercy is something received, never something achieved.

For people who had lost family ties, social standing, and civic acceptance, this was a profound reassurance. They had been removed from one community and welcomed into another. Whatever their neighbors thought, they now belonged to God.

wordNotes.term: οἱ οὐκ ἠλεημένοι νῦν δὲ ἐλεηθέντες (hoi ouk ēleēmenoi nyn de eleēthentes) — which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy
wordNotes.explanation: The contrast between a perfect participle and an aorist participle marks the change from a lasting condition of exclusion to a decisive act of divine mercy. The wording follows Hosea 2:23 and makes God’s compassion, not human merit, the basis of belonging.

verses.bibleText: Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With “Dearly beloved, I beseech you” Peter turns to a new stage of the letter. From here to 4:11 he applies the identity he has described to daily life among unbelievers. The tone is pastoral. He addresses them as people loved by God and by himself, and he urges rather than commands.

He calls them “strangers and pilgrims.” The first word described a resident alien, someone who lived in a place without full citizenship. The second described a temporary visitor passing through. Abraham called himself a stranger and sojourner when he bought a burial place in Canaan (Genesis 23:4), and David prayed as a stranger before God (Psalm 39:12). Believers belong to God’s holy nation (2:9), so their homeland is elsewhere. Their present society is a place where they live but where they do not finally belong.

That identity requires restraint: “abstain from fleshly lusts.” The phrase includes more than sexual sin. It covers every desire of fallen human nature that pulls against God, including the envy and strife that Paul lists among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:19-21). Such desires were part of the empty way of life they had inherited (1:14, 18).

These desires “war against the soul.” The verb is military, describing a campaign. The soul here means the whole person in relation to God, the life that God redeems and will raise. Peter does not set the body against an immortal inner part; he describes desires that lay siege to the whole self and seek to destroy it. Pilgrims cannot drift with the habits of the place they are passing through. They keep their eyes on the inheritance reserved in heaven (1:4) and live by the customs of their true homeland.

wordNotes.term: πάροικοι καὶ παρεπίδημοι (paroikoi kai parepidēmoi) — strangers and pilgrims
wordNotes.explanation: Paroikos denotes a resident foreigner without the full rights of a citizen. Parepidēmos describes a short-term visitor. Together, as in the Greek of Genesis 23:4 and Psalm 39:12, they describe believers whose present residence is real but whose citizenship and future belong to God.

wordNotes.term: στρατεύονται κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς (strateuontai kata tēs psychēs) — war against the soul
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to serve as a soldier or carry on a military campaign. Psychē here means the person’s life before God, the self whose salvation Peter has described. Fleshly desires besiege that life and aim at its ruin.

verses.bibleText: Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The positive side of verse 11 follows: “having your conversation honest among the Gentiles.” “Conversation” in the KJV means conduct, the whole manner of life. “Honest” translates a word meaning good in a visible, attractive way, the kind of goodness others can recognize. Peter calls unbelievers “the Gentiles” even though most of his readers were not Jewish by birth. Having become God’s people, they are no longer counted among the nations who do not know him.

The situation is hostile: “they speak against you as evildoers.” Christians in the provinces faced slander of many kinds. Because they refused to honor the city gods, they could be called godless. Because they withdrew from festivals, trade guild feasts, and temple banquets, they seemed antisocial and disloyal. Their private gatherings invited rumors of secret crimes. Peter does not advise them to withdraw further or to answer slander with slander. He calls them to live so well that the accusations fail.

“By your good works, which they shall behold.” The verb describes watching attentively over time, the observation of neighbors who see behavior day after day. Peter echoes the teaching of Jesus: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

The goal is that they may “glorify God in the day of visitation.” In Scripture God visits his people in grace and visits the unrepentant in judgment (Genesis 50:24; Isaiah 10:3). Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it did not know “the time of thy visitation” (Luke 19:44). Peter appears to hope that the observers of Christian conduct will be visited by God’s grace, turn to him, and glorify him. That hope also points toward the final day, when every person will stand before God. Faithful living now prepares the way for others to give him glory then, ideally as fellow worshipers.

wordNotes.term: ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπισκοπῆς (en hēmera episkopēs) — in the day of visitation
wordNotes.explanation: Episkopē speaks of God coming to inspect, to help, or to judge. In the Old Testament it can mean gracious intervention or reckoning. Here it most naturally describes the time when God draws near to those who have watched believers, bringing them to glorify him, with the final day in the background.

wordNotes.term: καλῶν ἔργων (kalōn ergōn) — good works
wordNotes.explanation: Kalos stresses goodness that is visible and admirable. Peter presents good works as the fruit of new birth, never the price of salvation, and expects them to commend the gospel to observers who are otherwise hostile.

verses.bibleText: Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now applies the call to honorable conduct to the first sphere of public life, the state. “Submit yourselves” means to take one’s proper place under an order of authority. It is a voluntary act, chosen by people who are free (2:16).

“Every ordinance of man” renders a phrase that reads literally “every human creation.” Peter calls government a human institution. He does not deny that God permits and uses rulers, as Paul stresses in Romans 13, but he places their authority firmly on the human level. The emperor, whatever titles he claimed, was a creature like anyone else.

The motive is “for the Lord’s sake.” Believers do not submit because rulers deserve it or because they fear punishment. They submit out of loyalty to Christ, who himself paid tribute, acknowledged that Pilate’s power had been given from above, and refused to lead an uprising (Matthew 22:21; John 19:11). Their conduct also guards the reputation of the Lord whose name they bear.

“The king, as supreme” refers to the Roman emperor, likely Nero at the time of writing, though before the worst of his violence against the church. Peter asks Christians to respect even a pagan ruler.

This submission has a boundary. Peter himself had told the council in Jerusalem, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). When rulers demand what God forbids, such as worship of other gods or violation of his commandments, believers obey God and accept the consequences without violence, as Daniel and his companions did (Daniel 3:16-18; 6:10). Even then they remain respectful. Submission does not mean surrendering conscience; it means honoring legitimate order while reserving final loyalty for God (2:17).

wordNotes.term: ὑποτάγητε (hypotagēte) — submit yourselves
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to arrange oneself under another within an ordered relationship. In the New Testament it describes a willing acceptance of one’s place, often for the sake of others and of the gospel. It governs the household instructions that follow (2:18; 3:1) and is distinct from blind obedience.

wordNotes.term: ἀνθρωπίνῃ κτίσει (anthrōpinē ktisei) — ordinance of man
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “human creation,” the phrase describes institutions established among people. By calling government human, Peter limits its claims. Rulers deserve respect, but they are not divine and cannot command the worship due to God alone.

verses.bibleText: Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Below the emperor stood the “governors,” the officials who administered provinces in his name. Pilate, Felix, and Festus held such positions in Judea. Peter’s readers would have known the governors of Bithynia, Asia, or Galatia as the visible face of Roman authority.

They are “sent by him,” commissioned by the emperor. Peter states the purpose of their office: “for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.” Government exists to restrain wrongdoing and to commend good conduct. Cities and rulers of the period often honored public benefactors with inscriptions and civic recognition, and Peter wants Christians to be among those whose behavior merits such praise.

Peter describes government as it ought to function. He knew from experience that officials could fail, for a Roman governor had condemned the innocent Jesus. Yet the failure of some rulers does not cancel the purpose of the office. Paul makes the same point in Romans 13:3-4. Believers should give authorities no legitimate reason to treat them as offenders and should support the order that protects the weak and permits the gospel to spread (1 Timothy 2:1-2).

wordNotes.term: εἰς ἔπαινον ἀγαθοποιῶν (eis epainon agathopoiōn) — for the praise of them that do well
wordNotes.explanation: Epainos is public commendation. Agathopoios describes one who does good. The phrase reflects the civic practice of honoring benefactors and states one aim of government: to encourage good conduct. Peter repeatedly urges believers to be known for doing good (2:15, 20; 3:6, 17).

verses.bibleText: For so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For so is the will of God” gives the deepest reason for submission. God himself wants his people to commend the gospel by their behavior. Their civic conduct is part of their obedience to him.

The means is “well doing,” the steady practice of good. The result is that they “put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.” The verb means to muzzle, as one muzzles an ox (1 Corinthians 9:9). Jesus silenced the Sadducees with the same word when they could no longer answer him (Matthew 22:34). The critics are described as foolish, lacking moral sense, and ignorant, speaking without knowing the truth about the people they accuse.

Peter’s strategy is striking. Slander is to be answered first by conduct. Argument has its place, and he will urge readiness to give a reason for hope (3:15), but words without a consistent life cannot silence accusation. A believer’s faithfulness at work, honesty in dealings, kindness to neighbors, and respect for authority leave the accuser with nothing to say. Over time, unfounded charges lose their force when they meet consistent goodness. Peter hopes for a silence of shame that may in time turn to faith (3:16).

wordNotes.term: φιμοῦν (phimoun) — put to silence
wordNotes.explanation: The verb literally means to muzzle and figuratively to reduce to silence. Peter pictures good conduct closing the mouths of slanderers, leaving their accusations without evidence.

wordNotes.term: ἀγνωσίαν (agnōsian) — ignorance
wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes a lack of knowledge, here a failure to understand the faith and life of Christians. Paul uses it for some who had no knowledge of God. Such ignorance fuels slander but can be dispelled by observed goodness.

verses.bibleText: As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter guards against two misunderstandings. Submission might seem to make believers servile, and Christian freedom might seem to excuse them from earthly obligations. He answers both with three phrases.

“As free.” Believers have been redeemed from the empty way of life handed down from their ancestors (1:18). The Son has made them free indeed (John 8:36). They submit to rulers as people who have a higher allegiance, not as people with no choice. Their submission is an act of freedom.

“Not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness.” A cloak covers what lies beneath. Some might claim spiritual liberty while hiding self-will, disrespect, or evil intent. The word “maliciousness” is the same one translated “malice” in verse 1. Freedom used as a pretext for wrongdoing is no freedom at all; Peter later describes false teachers who promise liberty while they themselves are slaves of corruption (2 Peter 2:19).

“But as the servants of God.” The word is literally “slaves.” Christian freedom is not independence from all authority. It is release from sin’s mastery into the service of God. Paul states the same paradox: the one called as a slave is the Lord’s freedman, and the one called as free is Christ’s slave (1 Corinthians 7:22). Because believers belong to God, no ruler owns their conscience. Because they belong to God, they also serve others gladly and honor the order he permits. Such free service gives the world a picture of God’s character, and the reputation of his name depends on how his servants live.

wordNotes.term: ἐλεύθεροι … θεοῦ δοῦλοι (eleutheroi … theou douloi) — free … servants of God
wordNotes.explanation: Eleutheros describes one who is not a slave. Doulos describes one who belongs to a master. Peter joins the two: believers are freed from the bondage of their former life precisely by belonging to God, and this belonging both liberates them and directs their freedom toward service.

wordNotes.term: ἐπικάλυμμα (epikalymma) — cloke
wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes a covering or veil and figuratively a pretext. Peter warns against using Christian liberty to conceal wrong motives or actions.

verses.bibleText: Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The paragraph closes with four short commands that summarize the believer’s relationships.

“Honour all men.” Every person deserves respect, including slaves, strangers, opponents, and persecutors. The basis is creation: every human being bears God’s image (Genesis 1:27; James 3:9). Christians who were themselves treated with contempt were not to return contempt.

“Love the brotherhood.” The word describes the community of believers as a family. Honor extends to everyone, but love of a particular, family kind binds those born of the same Father (1:22). Peter will later remind his readers that a whole brotherhood throughout the world shares their sufferings (5:9).

“Fear God.” Reverent awe belongs to God alone. Peter has already urged his readers to pass their time of sojourning in fear, mindful that the Father judges impartially (1:17).

“Honour the king.” The command uses the same verb as the first line. Proverbs 24:21 had said, “fear thou the LORD and the king.” Peter adjusts the pattern. Fear goes to God, while the king receives honor, the same honor given to all people. The emperor, who might claim divine reverence, is placed among human beings. Respect is due to him, worship is not. This small change shows how Peter can urge submission to authority and still keep every earthly power under God.

wordNotes.term: τὸν θεὸν φοβεῖσθε (ton theon phobeisthe) — fear God
wordNotes.explanation: Fear here is reverent awe and accountable devotion, the recognition that God is holy and judges justly. Peter reserves this attitude for God, while giving honor to rulers and all people.

wordNotes.term: ἀδελφότητα (adelphotēta) — the brotherhood
wordNotes.explanation: The noun refers to the fellowship of believers as a family of brothers and sisters. Peter uses it again of the worldwide church sharing in suffering, showing that believers belong to a community larger than their local congregation.

verses.bibleText: Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter turns to the household, the basic unit of ancient society, and addresses “servants” first. The word means household slaves, who might be cooks, tutors, stewards, nurses, or laborers. Ancient moral writers usually spoke to masters about how to manage slaves. Peter speaks to slaves directly, treating them as moral agents responsible to God. He addresses no masters at all, which suggests that the masters in view were mostly unbelievers.

“Be subject to your masters with all fear.” The fear is directed toward God, as in 1:17 and 2:17, rather than toward the master. Reverence for God governs how the slave serves. This reverence gives dignity to labor that society considered contemptible.

The instruction covers “not only … the good and gentle, but also … the froward.” Gentle masters were reasonable and fair. “Froward” translates a word meaning crooked, the term Peter used on the day of Pentecost for a perverse generation (Acts 2:40). A slave under such a master could be beaten, insulted, or ordered to share in idolatrous household rites, with little legal protection.

Peter does not defend slavery as an institution. He writes to people who could not change their social condition and shows them how to live faithfully within it. The gospel also carried seeds that would undermine slavery: in Christ there is neither bond nor free (Galatians 3:28); Onesimus was to be received as a brother beloved (Philemon 1:16); and slaves who could gain freedom were encouraged to take it (1 Corinthians 7:21). Submission never included sin; a Christian slave could not obey a command to worship idols.

The principle of faithful service under difficult authority applies to employees and others in subordinate positions today. It does not require anyone to remain in abuse when lawful protection is available, nor does it silence appeals for justice. It calls for integrity, diligence, and refusal to retaliate, because the believer serves Christ above every earthly master.

wordNotes.term: οἰκέται (oiketai) — servants
wordNotes.explanation: The word refers to household slaves, those who worked within a family’s domestic establishment. Jesus used it when he said no household servant can serve two masters. Peter addresses them as members of God’s people with full moral responsibility before him.

wordNotes.term: σκολιοῖς (skoliois) — froward
wordNotes.explanation: Skolios means crooked or bent, and figuratively perverse, unfair, or harsh. It describes masters whose treatment of slaves is twisted and unjust. Peter used the same word on the day of Pentecost.

verses.bibleText: For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For this is thankworthy.” The word is the common New Testament term for grace. Here it describes conduct that finds favor with God. Jesus used the same word when he asked what credit there is in loving only those who love you (Luke 6:32-34). Ordinary goodness to the kind wins no special approval; goodness toward the unkind reflects God’s own character.

The conduct God commends is that “a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully.” The motive is “conscience toward God,” literally an awareness of God. The believing slave endures unjust pain because he knows God sees, God cares, and God will judge rightly. Endurance without that awareness might be mere resignation or stubbornness. Endurance with it becomes an act of faith.

“Grief” refers to pain or sorrow. “Suffering wrongfully” means undeservedly, without having done wrong. Peter does not praise suffering in itself or call injustice good. He commends the faithful response of a person who suffers innocently and keeps trusting God rather than turning to bitterness or revenge. Such endurance is never solitary; the God who sees the wrong also supplies grace to bear it.

This principle reaches beyond slavery to every believer misjudged and mistreated for doing right. It prepares for Peter’s great example in verses 21-25, where the One who suffered most unjustly shows the way.

wordNotes.term: χάρις (charis) — thankworthy
wordNotes.explanation: Usually translated “grace,” charis here refers to what is pleasing and commendable before God. The word recurs in verse 20, where the KJV renders the phrase “acceptable with God.”

wordNotes.term: διὰ συνείδησιν θεοῦ (dia syneidēsin theou) — for conscience toward God
wordNotes.explanation: Syneidēsis can mean conscience or awareness. With “God” it describes a mind aware of God and his will. Such awareness enables a believer to endure unjust treatment as one who lives in God’s presence.

verses.bibleText: For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter sharpens the contrast with a question: “For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently?” “Glory” here means credit or renown. A slave who was lazy, dishonest, or disobedient and was punished for it gained no honor by bearing the punishment quietly. He received what he had earned.

“Buffeted” means struck with the fist. The same verb describes what was done to Jesus in the high priest’s house, when men spat in his face and beat him with their fists (Matthew 26:67; Mark 14:65). Peter, who stood in the courtyard that night, chooses a word that already points toward the example he is about to give.

The other case is different: “if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.” “Acceptable” repeats the word translated “thankworthy” in verse 19. Patient endurance of undeserved suffering wins God’s approval because it mirrors the way of Christ.

The verse also carries a warning. Believers must not confuse the consequences of their own wrongdoing with persecution for righteousness. Peter will say plainly that none should suffer as a thief or an evildoer (4:15). Nor should believers provoke hostility needlessly. The suffering God honors comes to those who are doing good.

wordNotes.term: κολαφιζόμενοι (kolaphizomenoi) — buffeted
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to strike with the fist, to beat or maltreat physically. It describes the abuse Jesus received during his trial and the hardships Paul endured as an apostle. Peter uses it of slaves beaten by masters.

wordNotes.term: τοῦτο χάρις παρὰ θεῷ (touto charis para theō) — this is acceptable with God
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “this is grace before God,” the phrase describes conduct that God regards with favor. It repeats the language of verse 19 and frames the paragraph around the approval of God, which outweighs the approval or disapproval of human masters.

verses.bibleText: For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For even hereunto were ye called.” The calling that brought believers out of darkness into light (2:9) includes the way of patient suffering for doing good. Peter says the same elsewhere: believers are called to bless those who revile them (3:9), and the God of all grace has called them to eternal glory after they have suffered a while (5:10). Suffering for righteousness is not an accident outside God’s purpose. It belongs to the path of discipleship.

The reason is “because Christ also suffered for us.” Many manuscripts read “for you,” bringing the point home to the readers. The words “for you” mean on your behalf. Before Christ is an example, he is a substitute. He suffered so that those who had wandered could be brought back to God (2:24-25; 3:18). His suffering is the ground of their salvation, and only then the pattern for their lives.

He left “an example.” The Greek word described a model of letters written by a teacher so that a child could trace over them and learn to write. Christ’s conduct under suffering is the pattern believers trace, stroke by stroke, in their own responses to injustice.

“That ye should follow his steps.” The word “steps” means footprints. Believers walk where Jesus walked, placing their feet in his tracks. The image recalls Jesus’ call to his disciples to deny themselves, take up the cross, and follow him (Matthew 16:24).

The words carry personal weight for Peter. When Jesus first spoke of his coming suffering, Peter rebuked him and was himself rebuked (Matthew 16:21-23). After the resurrection, Jesus told Peter how he would die and then said, “Follow me” (John 21:18-19). The apostle who once resisted the way of the cross now urges suffering slaves, and all believers, to walk in it. The slave’s situation becomes a model for the whole church, since every believer is a servant of God (2:16) who may be treated unjustly for doing right.

wordNotes.term: ὑπογραμμόν (hypogrammon) — an example
wordNotes.explanation: The word referred to a writing model, letters traced for a pupil to copy. Applied to Christ, it presents his conduct as a pattern believers reproduce in their own lives. It does not make Christ merely a moral teacher; his example rests on his saving suffering “for you.”

wordNotes.term: ἐπακολουθήσητε τοῖς ἴχνεσιν (epakolouthēsēte tois ichnesin) — follow his steps
wordNotes.explanation: Ichnos means a footprint or track. The verb means to follow closely after. The image is of disciples walking in the very tracks left by their Master, sharing his path of obedience and suffering.

verses.bibleText: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter now draws on Isaiah 53, the song of the Suffering Servant, to describe the example he has just mentioned. “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” follows Isaiah 53:9.

The first clause declares Christ’s sinlessness. Peter had lived with Jesus for years and watched him under every kind of pressure. His testimony agrees with the rest of the New Testament: Jesus was tempted in all points as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15); he knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21); in him is no sin (1 John 3:5). Even Pilate found no fault in him (John 18:38). His suffering was therefore unjust in the fullest sense, and his sinlessness qualified him to be the lamb without blemish and without spot (1:19).

The second clause turns to speech. Under interrogation, mockery, and pain, Jesus never used deceit to escape suffering. This ties the chapter together: believers are to lay aside all guile (2:1) because their Lord had none.

wordNotes.term: οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος (oude heurethē dolos) — neither was guile found
wordNotes.explanation: Dolos is deceit or treachery. The verb “was found” suggests examination: however closely his words were tested, no deception appeared. The phrase from Isaiah 53:9 also describes the redeemed who follow the Lamb.

verses.bibleText: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter recalls how Jesus responded to the abuse of his trial and crucifixion. “When he was reviled, reviled not again.” He was mocked by soldiers, taunted by priests, insulted by passersby, and scorned even by a crucified criminal, yet he did not answer insult with insult. Isaiah had foreseen it: the Servant was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth, like a lamb led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7). Before the high priest and before Pilate, Jesus kept silent in the face of false accusation (Mark 14:61; 15:5).

“When he suffered, he threatened not.” Victims of injustice often threaten their persecutors with future revenge or divine retribution. Jesus did neither. From the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

This restraint was not passivity or weakness. When struck, Jesus could ask calmly why he was being struck if he had spoken rightly (John 18:23). He spoke truth when truth needed to be spoken. What he refused was retaliation. Peter himself had once drawn a sword in the garden and been told to put it away (John 18:10-11). He now writes as one who learned that lesson.

The key to such restraint is the final clause: he “committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.” The word “himself” is supplied by the translators; the verb may also mean that he entrusted his cause, or even his tormentors, to God. The imperfect tense suggests a continual handing over throughout his ordeal. Jesus could refuse revenge because he was certain that God would judge justly. Vengeance belongs to the Lord, who will repay (Romans 12:19).

Believers who suffer unjustly can follow the same path. They may speak the truth and seek justice where it is available, but they leave final judgment with God. Peter will close his teaching on suffering with the same counsel: commit the keeping of your souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator (4:19).

wordNotes.term: λοιδορούμενος οὐκ ἀντελοιδόρει (loidoroumenos ouk anteloidorei) — when he was reviled, reviled not again
wordNotes.explanation: Loidoreō means to insult or abuse verbally. The compound with anti- means to insult in return. Jesus endured insult without answering in kind, and Peter calls believers to the same response.

wordNotes.term: παρεδίδου τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως (paredidou tō krinonti dikaiōs) — committed himself to him that judgeth righteously
wordNotes.explanation: Paradidōmi means to hand over or entrust. The imperfect tense pictures repeated or continual entrusting. Jesus placed himself and his cause in the hands of God, the just Judge, trusting him to vindicate the right.

verses.bibleText: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Peter’s description of Christ’s example now moves beyond example. “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree” describes what no disciple can imitate. Drawing on Isaiah 53:4 and 53:12, he declares that Christ carried our sins. In Isaiah the Servant bears the sin of many and is wounded for the transgressions of others. The language is substitutionary. He who did no sin (2:22) took on himself the guilt and penalty that belonged to sinners.

“His own self” stresses that this was personal. No animal and no representative took his place; he bore it himself. “In his own body” stresses the physical reality of the cross. Christ’s sacrifice was not merely an idea or a symbol. “On the tree” recalls the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23 on anyone hanged on a tree. Peter used the same expression in his early preaching (Acts 5:30; 10:39), and Paul explains that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The verb translated “bare” is also used in the Greek Old Testament for carrying a sacrifice up to the altar, and the cross can be seen as the altar on which the true sacrifice was offered.

The purpose follows: “that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness.” Christ’s death aims at more than pardon. Its goal is a transformed life. The word “being dead” means having parted from or ceased to have any part in sins. Believers have been separated from their old relation to sin and now live in harmony with God’s righteousness. Paul says the same: reckon yourselves dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ (Romans 6:11). Forgiveness and transformation flow from the same cross.

“By whose stripes ye were healed” quotes Isaiah 53:5. The word “stripes” refers to the welt or bruise left by a blow or a whip. Slaves in Peter’s audience knew such wounds. Peter tells them that the wounds of their Lord have healed them. The healing is primarily spiritual: the wound of sin, which separated them from God and corrupted their lives, has been treated at its root. Christ’s ministry included physical healing as a sign of this deeper restoration, and the complete healing of body and soul awaits the resurrection at his return. Peter changes Isaiah’s “we” to “ye,” addressing his readers directly.

The once-for-all sacrifice on the cross is complete. Its benefits are now applied by the risen Christ, who appears in the presence of God for us as our High Priest (Hebrews 9:24-28).

wordNotes.term: ἀνήνεγκεν … ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον (anēnenken … epi to xylon) — bare … on the tree
wordNotes.explanation: Anapherō can mean to bear or carry up, and in sacrificial contexts to offer up on an altar. Isaiah 53:12 LXX uses it for the Servant bearing the sins of many. Xylon, wood or tree, recalls the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23. Together the words describe Christ carrying sin to the cross as the substitute for sinners.

wordNotes.term: ἀπογενόμενοι (apogenomenoi) — being dead
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to depart from, to cease to have a part in, and by extension to die to something. Peter uses it to describe the believer’s separation from the dominion of sin as the result of Christ’s death, leading to a new life lived for righteousness.

verses.bibleText: For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For ye were as sheep going astray” continues to draw on Isaiah 53, this time verse 6: “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way.” The tense pictures a continual wandering. Before conversion, Peter’s readers were lost, scattered, and exposed to danger, each going his own way. Sheep that wander do not find their way home by themselves.

“But are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.” The verb “returned” is the common word for turning or being turned back, the language of conversion (Acts 3:19). It may be read as passive, “you have been turned back,” emphasizing the Shepherd’s initiative in seeking the lost. Jesus spoke of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one that strayed (Luke 15:4-6).

“Shepherd” recalls God’s role as the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23:1; Ezekiel 34:11-16), a role Jesus claimed as the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). “Bishop” translates a word meaning overseer or guardian, one who watches over others for their good. In Ezekiel 34 God promised to seek, gather, and watch over his scattered flock himself. Peter sees that promise fulfilled in Christ.

The risen Lord once told Peter three times to feed his sheep (John 21:15-17), and Peter will later urge elders to shepherd the flock until the chief Shepherd appears (5:2-4). Here, at the end of a chapter addressed to slaves who had little protection from earthly masters, Peter reminds them that they have a Guardian whose care is constant and whose authority is final.

wordNotes.term: ἐπεστράφητε (epestraphēte) — are now returned
wordNotes.explanation: Epistrephō means to turn around or return, and in the New Testament it often describes conversion. The passive form may stress being turned back by God’s action. Jesus used the same verb when he told Peter, “when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.”

wordNotes.term: ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον (poimena kai episkopon) — Shepherd and Bishop
wordNotes.explanation: Poimēn means shepherd and episkopos means overseer or guardian. Both titles describe Christ’s caring authority over his people. They fulfill God’s promise in Ezekiel 34 to shepherd and watch over his scattered flock himself.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When the people around you misunderstand or reject your faith, whose verdict about your worth do you live by?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Those reborn through Christ are God’s chosen and priestly people, and they display that identity by craving the Lord, living honorably under authority, and following the pattern of Christ’s patient, atoning suffering.
discussionQuestions: Why does Peter place the vices of verse 1 immediately after the command to love in 1:22?
What does it mean that every believer belongs to a holy priesthood, and what sacrifices does that priesthood offer?
How does the stone that is precious to some become a stumbling stone to others?
Where does submission to human authority reach its limit, and how does fearing God set that limit?
How do verses 21-25 keep Christ’s example and Christ’s substitution together?
commonMisunderstandings: Being a royal priesthood does not abolish Christ’s unique mediation; believers come to God only through him.
The appointment in verse 8 describes the fixed outcome of rejecting Christ, not an arbitrary decree that some must disbelieve.
Submission to rulers is never a duty to disobey God, and the instructions to slaves do not approve of slavery or require anyone to seek out abuse.
Christ’s example does not replace his atoning death; Peter grounds imitation in the fact that he bore our sins.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep identity and conduct together: God first declares who his people are in Christ, and that identity then shapes how they speak, worship, submit, and suffer.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Come again today to the living Stone, let him build you into his house, and walk in the footsteps of the Shepherd who bore your sins and brought you home.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Christ, the stone rejected by men and chosen by God, bore our sins on the cross so that straying people might be healed, returned to God, and made part of his own people.
flow: Like sheep, all of us have wandered from God and cannot heal ourselves.
God laid in Zion a precious cornerstone, Jesus Christ, whom people rejected and God raised.
On the cross he bore our sins in his own body, so that by his wounds we are healed.
Whoever trusts him will not be put to shame but receives mercy and becomes part of God’s people.
The one who comes to the Shepherd begins a new life of dying to sin and living to righteousness.
simpleIllustrations: A child learning to write traces letters drawn by the teacher; Christ’s life is the pattern believers trace, yet he first wrote our pardon with his own blood.
A building stone discarded by careless workmen may be chosen by the architect to hold the whole structure together; God made the rejected Jesus the cornerstone of his house.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop wandering and return today to the Shepherd and Overseer of your soul?
cautions: Do not present conversion as joining a respectable social group; Peter expects believers to be misunderstood.
Do not use the passage to tell victims of abuse that God requires them to remain in danger.
Do not present healing in verse 24 as a promise that every bodily illness will now be removed.

reflectionQuestions: Which of the attitudes in verse 1 most often damages my relationships with other believers?
Do I long for the Lord with anything like the hunger of a newborn for milk?
What spiritual sacrifices have I offered to God this week through Jesus Christ?
How would my neighbors describe my conduct if they observed it closely over time?
When I am treated unjustly, do I commit my cause to the righteous Judge or try to settle it myself?
